steps.prompt: How do you decide — on ONE page — whether an AI product is worth building, and how not to ship a confidently wrong one?
steps.sub: This is the capstone. Everything from the course — feasibility, data, metrics, responsible AI, ops — folds into a single reusable one-pager you fill in before any AI product. By the end you'll know all 8 sections in order, why the METRIC is the most dangerous line on the page, and you'll have scoped a real product of your own with it.

steps.prompt: The AIPM one-pager — 8 sections, top to bottom.
steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the whole page.

cards.b: The job-to-be-done, for whom — and the COST of being wrong. A wrong loan denial costs more than a wrong song recommendation.
Three gates: does a pattern exist, does data exist, are errors tolerable? If any is 'no', stop or use rules.
Sources, rights/consent, who labels it, how fresh it stays, where the bias gaps are.
Non-ML baseline FIRST. Then model family / build-buy-API. For GenAI, climb the rung: prompt → RAG → fine-tune.
A business metric + a model metric + a GUARDRAIL metric. And how you'll A/B test it.
Fairness, privacy, explainability, human-in-the-loop — with a named owner.
Monitoring, drift detection, retraining cadence, and a rollback plan for when it goes wrong.
What kills this product — and what the first-run feels like BEFORE the model is any good.

steps.prompt: Put the 8 sections of the one-pager in the order you fill them in.
steps.sub: Tap them top-to-bottom, the way the page reads.
steps.why: Problem first (you can't judge anything without the job-to-be-done), then 'is AI even right', then the data that makes it possible, then approach, then how you'll measure it, then the responsible-AI gate, then ops to keep it alive, and finally the risks/cold-start reality check. Each section depends on the ones above it — that's why the order is the order.
hints: You can't pick metrics or data before you know the PROBLEM and whether AI is the right tool at all.
Build → measure → govern → operate → stress-test: Approach, then Metrics, then Responsible-AI, then Ops, then Risks.

steps.prompt: Section 2 asks 'is AI the right tool?'. Which situation should make you walk away (or use plain rules)?
steps.sub: One of these fails a gate.

options.t: Lots of clean historical examples exist and the pattern is learnable.
There's no underlying pattern — outcomes are essentially random — yet a single wrong call is catastrophic.
The task has a real pattern and occasional small errors are tolerable.

steps.why: AI learns patterns from data. If there's NO pattern to learn AND errors aren't tolerable, you've failed two gates at once — a model will just launder randomness into confident-looking output. That's the worst case: it looks intelligent while being noise. The other two situations are exactly where AI fits.
hints: AI needs a pattern to exist and errors to be survivable. Which option has neither?
A model trained on randomness still outputs confident answers — that's the trap.

steps.prompt: Section 5 is a trap. The metric IS the product spec.
steps.sub: Tap each card — this is the heart of the lesson.

cards.h: The model optimizes EXACTLY what you measure
cards.b: Not what you meant — what you wrote down. The metric isn't a report card; it's the instruction the optimizer obeys literally.

cards.h: A wrong metric → a confidently wrong product
cards.b: Optimize 'watch time' and you may get rage-bait. Optimize 'tickets closed' and the bot closes them WITHOUT solving anything. It hits your number and fails the user.

cards.h: So you ALSO define a guardrail metric
cards.b: A second number that must NOT get worse while the main metric climbs. It's the leash on gaming — e.g. 'watch time up, BUT reported-content rate flat'.

steps.prompt: TrigunAI's drone story. The RL policy's numerical REWARD dropped from epoch 100 to epoch 500, but a separate VLM judge rated the 500-iter flight visually BETTER. What's the real lesson?
steps.sub: This is the metric trap in the wild. Pick the deepest reading.

options.t: The VLM judge was broken — trust the reward number, it's the objective truth.
The reward measures what PPO optimizes (a formula); the VLM measures what humans actually value. They diverge by design — so you need an eye OUTSIDE the optimizer.
Training failed — a falling reward always means the model got worse.

steps.why: The reward number is just the formula the optimizer maximizes — it is NOT a measure of 'good flying'. The policy can score lower on the formula while flying in a way humans judge as cleaner. That gap is the whole point: if your only judge is the thing being optimized, you can't catch the case where it games the metric. The VLM is the guardrail/outside-eye. Same reason an AIPM never lets the model's own optimization target be the sole definition of success.
hints: Reward = the formula PPO is climbing. Is that the same thing as 'looks like good flying' to a human?
When the optimizer grades its own work, who catches the gaming? You need a judge it can't optimize against.

steps.prompt: Run a real product through the one-pager: 'Acharya should auto-grade student answers.'
steps.sub: You're the AIPM. Pick the right call at each section.
steps.goal: Scope Acharya auto-grading section-by-section, choosing the responsible call each time.

turns.situation: Section 1 — Problem & user. Acharya tutors students on WhatsApp; grading every free-text answer by hand doesn't scale. A wrong grade can discourage a learner or pass someone who didn't get it.
turns.q: What belongs on the 'cost of being wrong' line?
options: A wrong grade demoralizes a correct student or gives false confidence to a confused one — high human cost, so errors are NOT cheap.
There is no cost; it's just a number.
The only cost is server time.
turns.log: 📒 §1 Problem: scale grading; cost-of-wrong = damaged trust + mis-taught learner → errors matter

turns.situation: Section 2 — Is AI the right tool? Grading short conceptual answers has a learnable pattern (we have past graded answers), and a human can review borderline cases.
options: Pattern exists + data exists + errors tolerable (with a human reviewing low-confidence ones) → AI fits, with a human in the loop.
No pattern exists, so don't build it.
Skip the gates — auto-grading is obviously fine.
turns.log: 📒 §2 Fit: yes — pattern + data + tolerable errors, gated by human review on low confidence

turns.situation: Section 4 — Approach. The team wants to fine-tune a model on day one.
options: Start with a baseline: a prompt that asks an LLM to grade against a rubric. Only climb to RAG (pull the rubric/model answer) or fine-tuning if the baseline isn't good enough.
Fine-tune immediately — baselines are a waste of time.
Build a custom model from scratch before trying anything simpler.
turns.log: 📒 §4 Approach: baseline = rubric prompt; climb prompt→RAG→fine-tune only if needed

turns.situation: Section 5 — Success metrics. Someone proposes optimizing for 'agreement with the answer key'.
turns.q: What's missing, and why is a guardrail vital here?
options: Add a guardrail: false-pass rate on confused students must stay low. Pure 'agreement with key' can be gamed by always grading lenient — students feel good, learn nothing.
Agreement with the key is enough on its own.
Drop metrics entirely; trust the model.
turns.log: ✅ §5 Metrics: business (less manual grading) + model (agreement) + GUARDRAIL (false-pass rate flat) + A/B vs human grader

hints: At each step, the responsible AIPM call is the one that respects the human cost and resists shortcuts.
Section 4 is always 'baseline first'; Section 5 always needs a guardrail next to the headline metric.

steps.prompt: Sort each line into the right section of the one-pager.
steps.sub: Tap a line, then its section. This is the whole page in practice.

items.t: 'Do we have consent to use these chat logs for training?'
'Watch the false-pass rate so the model can't game leniency.'
'A named owner reviews fairness across student languages.'
'Alert if grading accuracy drifts after a new student cohort joins.'
'Are any student groups missing from our labeled examples?'
'One-tap rollback to the previous model if quality drops.'
'Business metric: hours of manual grading saved per week.'

hints: Consent, labels, and bias gaps live in the Data plan; drift, alerts, and rollback live in Ops.
Anything about WHO is treated fairly + a named owner is the Responsible-AI gate; numbers you optimize/protect are Metrics.

statements.t: You should try a non-ML baseline before reaching for a model.
statements.why: Yes — the baseline tells you whether ML even earns its complexity, and gives you a number to beat.

statements.t: A model optimizes what you intended, not what you literally measured.
statements.why: False — it optimizes the measured metric LITERALLY. That gap between intent and metric is the central AIPM failure mode.

statements.t: A guardrail metric exists to catch the main metric being gamed.
statements.why: Right — it's the second number that must not degrade while the headline metric climbs, your leash on gaming.

statements.t: If the model's own training reward goes up, the product is definitely better for users.
statements.why: False — the drone case proved reward and human value can diverge. You need a judge outside the optimizer.

statements.t: The responsible-AI gate should have a named owner, not just a checklist.
statements.why: Yes — fairness/privacy/explainability without an accountable owner is a checkbox nobody enforces.

hints: Two of these are the metric trap restated — both are false.
Baseline-first, guardrails, and a named owner are all things this lesson said to DO.

steps.prompt: Make it yours — name the product you'll scope.
steps.sub: Not graded. Pick a real one; the one-pager only works on something concrete.

fields.label: What AI product or feature will YOU scope with this one-pager?
fields.ph: e.g. auto-tag support tickets, recommend the next lesson, draft sales replies

fields.label: For that product, what's the GUARDRAIL metric — the number that must not get worse?
fields.ph: e.g. false-escalation rate, unsubscribe rate, fairness gap across user groups

steps.prompt: Lock it in: tap EVERY true statement about the AIPM one-pager.
chips: Section 1 names the user, the job, and the cost of being wrong
Approach starts with a non-ML baseline before a model
Metrics pair a headline metric with a guardrail metric
A model optimizes exactly what you measure, not what you meant
If training reward rises, you never need a judge outside the optimizer
steps.why: The first four are the spine of the page: define the user and the cost of error, baseline before modeling, headline + guardrail metrics, and the hard truth that the model obeys the metric literally. The last is false — the drone reward-vs-VLM divergence is exactly why you keep an eye outside the optimizer.
hints: Four of these you just ordered, traced, and sorted.
Which statement contradicts the drone reward-vs-VLM story?
